title: QWS v DIRECTOR GENERAL OF HEALTH
text:
IN THE EMPLOYMENT RELATIONS AUTHORITY
AUCKLAND
I TE RATONGA AHUMANA TAIMAHI
TĀMAKI MAKAURAU ROHE
[2026] NZERA 511
3174644
BETWEEN QWS
Applicant
AND DIRECTOR GENERAL OF
HEALTH
Respondent
Member of Authority: Marija Urlich
Representatives: Jane Carrigan, advocate for the Applicant
Bronwyn Heenan and Tim Bremner, counsel for the

Investigation Meeting: On the papers
Determination: 31 July 2026
DETERMINATION OF THE AUTHORITY
Employment Relationship Problem
[1] This determination concerns whether the Authority has jurisdiction to
investigate and determine QWS’s application given s 142 of the Act which provides:1
No action may be commenced in the Authority or the court in relation
to an employment relationship problem that is not a personal grievance
more than 6 years after the date on which the cause of action arose.
The Authority’s investigation
[2] By consent this matter is determined on the papers. The parties have filed
information and submissions as directed. As permitted by s 174E of the Employment
Relations Act 2000 (the Act) this determination has stated findings of fact and law,
1 Employment Relations Act 2000, s 142.

expressed conclusions on issues necessary to dispose of the matter and specified orders
made. It has not recorded all evidence and submissions received. In determining this
matter, the Authority has carefully considered all the material before it, including all
information provided by the parties and their submissions.
Interim non-publication order
[3] The interim non-publication order relating to the name and identity of the
application dated 23 June 2026 is to remain in place: clause 10, schedule 2, Employment
Relations Act 2000. Leave is granted for the parties to apply for that order to be made
permanent.
Issues
[4] The issue identified is whether the Authority has jurisdiction to investigate and
determine QWS’s employment relationship problem or whether it is time-barred by s
142 of the Act.
Relevant law
[5] There is a six-year limit on bringing an action in relation to an employment
relationship problem that is not a personal grievance.2 There is no express power to
extend this time limit.3 The time extension discretions in sections 219 or 221(c) of the
Act are not available in a s 142 consideration.4 When a cause of action can be said to
arise is a matter of the reasonable discoverability of “knowledge (actual or constructive)
of the material facts that make up the claim”.5
Background
[6] QWS had a profoundly disabled child for whom, from birth, they provided a
very high level of disability support and care. QWS’s child died on 16 May 2016. On 7
June 2022 QWS filed an application in the Authority seeking a range of orders
including:6
(i) a declaration they were an employee of the (then named) respondent;
2 Employment Relations Act 2000, s 142.
3 Blue Water Hotel Ltd v VBS [2018] NZEmpC 128 at [96].
4 Maharaj v Wesley Wellington Mission Inc [2016] NZEmpC 129.
5 Labour Inspector v Temple [2026] NZEmpC 109 at [61].
6 An amendment statement of problem was filed 8 August 2022

(ii) wage and holiday pay arrears;
(iii) personal grievances “raised within 90 days on each occasion and over a
period of 19 years”; and
(iv) penalties for statutory breaches.
[7] The Authority’s investigation of this matter was stayed pending resolution of
other proceedings.7
Discussion
[8] QWS says an employment relationship was not reasonably discoverable until
some time after 16 May 2016. They say theirs is not an ordinary employment dispute.
They knew they were a carer but did not and could not have known the relationship was
capable of being one of employment. Now that position has been confirmed by the
Supreme Court, it is unfair and unreasonable for the Crown to contend that they could
have known their legal position earlier. QWS says they were subject to extraordinary
personal, emotional and physical circumstances while providing full-time disability
support services and, along with the circumstances after the death of their child, are part
of the relevant factual matrix within which they ask the Authority to exercise its
discretion.
[9] The matter QWS seeks to bring before the Authority arises from the care and
support they provided to their child during their lifetime for which they seek orders
including a declaration of status as an employee and wage arrears. It is as a matter of
logic an employment relationship problem.
[10] In the circumstances of this employment relationship problem, the asserted
employment relationship must have ended on 16 May 2016 because after that date,
QWS’s day-to-day caring and support work came to an end. The application,
subsequently lodged in the Authority was outside the six-year limit.
[11] The Authority has no discretion to extend the s 142 six-year time limit. There is
no exceptional circumstance discretion that I can exercise in respect of the six-year
limitation period. The considerations QWS says are relevant – length of delay,
7 Fleming v Attorney-General [2025] NZSC 188.

explanation for delay, prejudice, conduct, interest of justice – are not available in this
context because there is no discretion to exercise.
[12] The next issue to consider is whether the course of action was reasonably
discoverable within the six years preceding filing of the matter in the Authority.
[13] In Labour Inspector v Temple the Chief Judge determined that in respect of a
wage arrears employment relationship problem, the correct basis to assess when the
cause of action arose is reasonable discoverability of the breach or, in other words,
when the employee had knowledge (actual or constructive) of the material facts that
make up the claim for wage arrears.8 In Temple the Court found the clock started ticking
for the plaintiffs to bring their claims once they left a community where they were
indoctrinated, unable to access legal advice or information and were prohibited from
complaining to external authorities.9
[14] The information before the Authority indicates QWS was aware of the material
facts of employment as they related to their circumstances during the time they say they
were an employee. In the second amended statement of problem, they state they were a
full time carer of a disabled family member whose care needs continued into adulthood,
they sought funding under the disability framework, the Crown was aware they were a
full-time carer, providing funding for some of the time under a purported employment
framework and the Crown or its agents exercised employer type control over them by
way of funding mechanisms.10 Further, QWS’ statement of problem states they raised
multiple personal grievances with the putative employer during their years of care
giving.
[15] There can be no doubt QWS worked tirelessly to support and care for their child.
This included both the day-to-day requirements of caring for a person with complex
intellectual and physical needs and engaging with multiple agencies to advocate on their
behalf to access health care and support services and funding. QWS’ circumstances
were not of the type as found in Temple where the plaintiffs’ circumstances impaired
8 Labour Inspector v Temple [2026] NZEmpC 109, [58] – [61].
9 Ibid [66] – [69].
10 Second amended statement of problem 22 June 2026 at [2.2].

their ability to acquire knowledge of the material
facts
problems.
[16] QWS is time barred from seeking a
determination
personal grievance and penalty claims are also
barred
the declaration of employment status.
Outcome
[17] The Authority cannot investigate and
relationship problem because it is time-barred.
Costs
[18] Costs are reserved.
